Assignment 4: Text and Sequence Data¶

Learned embedding layer vs. pretrained GloVe embeddings on IMDB when training data is limited¶

Python 3, TensorFlow / Keras 3

Task. Re-run the IMDB example from Chollet's Deep Learning with Python (chapter 6 in the 1st edition, chapter 11 in the 2nd edition, which is the version used in the module slides) with these changes:

# Requirement Where it is handled
1 Cut reviews off after 150 words TextVectorization(output_sequence_length=150)
2 Restrict training samples to 100 Experiment 1
3 Validate on 10,000 samples one fixed set of 10,000 held-out reviews, used in every run
4 Only the top 10,000 words TextVectorization(max_tokens=10000)
5 Embedding layer vs. pretrained embedding, then vary the number of training samples Experiments 1 and 2

Model. The bidirectional LSTM from the slides: integer sequence → Embedding → Bidirectional(LSTM(32)) → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(1, sigmoid). Only the embedding changes between the three versions I compare:

  1. Learned embedding. A 128-dimensional Embedding layer trained from scratch.
  2. GloVe (frozen). 100-dimensional GloVe 6B vectors loaded into the Embedding layer with trainable=False, as in the slides.
  3. GloVe (fine-tuned). The same GloVe starting point, but the vectors are allowed to update. I added this third version because it is a common way to get more out of a small dataset, and the module asks how performance can be improved with limited data.

What is different from the textbook run. Besides the required changes, I repeat each training size with several random seeds and keep a separate 10,000-review test set. With only 100 training reviews the accuracy moves a lot from one run to the next, so a single run per setting is not enough to say which embedding is better.

1. Setup¶

2. Data¶

IMDB: the Stanford Large Movie Review Dataset (Maas et al., 2011): 50,000 reviews, 25,000 positive / 25,000 negative. GloVe: glove.6B.100d (Pennington et al., 2014): 400,000 words × 100 dimensions, trained on Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5.

The original Stanford servers are frequently unreachable, so the notebook downloads byte-identical public mirrors: the imdb-data npm package (all 50,000 reviews in JSON) and the glove-wiki-gigaword-100 release of the gensim-data project (the 6B‑100d vectors with a one-line word2vec header).

In [8]:

2.1 Train / validation / test split¶

The 50,000 reviews are shuffled once (fixed seed) and split into:

  • Validation set (10,000 reviews), requirement 3. Used for early stopping and reported as validation accuracy.
  • Test set (10,000 reviews). Never used for any decision; it confirms that validation accuracy is not inflated by choosing the best epoch on the validation set.
  • Training pool (30,000 reviews). All training subsets (25 up to 20,000) are drawn from this pool.
In [10]:
rng_split = np.random.default_rng(SPLIT_SEED)
perm = rng_split.permutation(len(texts))
val_idx, test_idx, pool_idx = perm[:N_VAL], perm[N_VAL:N_VAL + N_TEST], perm[N_VAL + N_TEST:]

pd.DataFrame({
    "split": ["training pool", "validation", "test"],
    "reviews": [len(pool_idx), len(val_idx), len(test_idx)],
    "positive share": [labels[pool_idx].mean(), labels[val_idx].mean(), labels[test_idx].mean()],
}).round(3)

2.2 Text vectorisation (standardise → tokenise → index)¶

Following the slides, a TextVectorization layer:

  • standardises: lower-case, strips the <br /> HTML tags that IMDB reviews contain, removes punctuation;
  • tokenises on whitespace (word level, which sequence models need);
  • indexes the top 10,000 words (index 0 = padding/mask, 1 = [UNK] out-of-vocabulary);
  • truncates/pads every review to 150 tokens.

The vocabulary is built from the text of the 30,000-review training pool, with no labels involved. If it were built from only 100 reviews it would contain about 3,000 words, and the "top 10,000 words" requirement could not be met. The validation and test texts are never seen while the vocabulary is built.

In [11]:
def standardize(x):
    x = tf.strings.lower(x)
    x = tf.strings.regex_replace(x, r"<br\s*/?>", " ")
    x = tf.strings.regex_replace(x, r"[^a-z0-9' ]", " ")
    return x

vectorizer = layers.TextVectorization(max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS, output_mode="int",
                                      output_sequence_length=MAX_LEN, standardize=standardize)
vectorizer.adapt(tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(texts[pool_idx]).batch(1024))
vocab = [str(w) for w in vectorizer.get_vocabulary()]

def vectorize(arr):
    return np.concatenate([vectorizer(tf.constant(arr[i:i + 2048])).numpy()
                           for i in range(0, len(arr), 2048)])

X_pool, y_pool = vectorize(texts[pool_idx]), labels[pool_idx]
X_val,  y_val  = vectorize(texts[val_idx]),  labels[val_idx]
X_test, y_test = vectorize(texts[test_idx]), labels[test_idx]

truncated = np.mean([len(t.split()) > MAX_LEN for t in texts[val_idx]])
print("Vocabulary size:", len(vocab), "| first entries:", vocab[:12])
print("Tensor shapes  :", X_pool.shape, X_val.shape, X_test.shape)
print(f"Share of reviews longer than {MAX_LEN} words (i.e. truncated): {truncated:.1%}")
print("\nFirst review as integer indices (first 20):", X_val[0][:20])

2.3 Pretrained GloVe embedding matrix¶

Each of the 10,000 vocabulary words is looked up in GloVe, giving a (10000, 100) matrix. Words missing from GloVe, plus the padding and [UNK] rows, stay all-zero (as in the slides).

In [12]:
glove = {}
with gzip.open(glove_gz, "rt", encoding="utf8") as f:
    next(f)  # skip the word2vec header line "400000 100"
    for line in f:
        word, coefs = line.split(maxsplit=1)
        glove[word] = coefs
print(f"GloVe vectors loaded: {len(glove):,}")

embedding_matrix = np.zeros((MAX_TOKENS, EMBED_DIM_GLOVE), dtype="float32")
hits = 0
for i, word in enumerate(vocab[:MAX_TOKENS]):
    if i < 2:
        continue  # 0 = padding, 1 = [UNK]
    vec = glove.get(word)
    if vec is not None:
        embedding_matrix[i] = np.fromstring(vec, dtype="float32", sep=" ")
        hits += 1
del glove
print(f"Vocabulary words found in GloVe: {hits:,} / {MAX_TOKENS - 2:,} ({hits / (MAX_TOKENS - 2):.1%})")

GloVe vectors loaded: 400,000
Vocabulary words found in GloVe: 9,817 / 9,998 (98.2%)

3. Models¶

One builder, three embedding strategies. All three share the same BiLSTM + dropout + sigmoid head, so the only thing that changes is the embedding. mask_zero=True tells the LSTM to skip the padding positions (slides: masking).

In [13]:
ARMS = ["Learned embedding", "GloVe (frozen)", "GloVe (fine-tuned)"]

def build_model(arm):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int64")
    if arm == "Learned embedding":
        emb = layers.Embedding(MAX_TOKENS, EMBED_DIM_LEARNED, mask_zero=True)
    else:
        emb = layers.Embedding(MAX_TOKENS, EMBED_DIM_GLOVE, mask_zero=True,
                               embeddings_initializer=keras.initializers.Constant(embedding_matrix),
                               trainable=(arm == "GloVe (fine-tuned)"))
    x = emb(inputs)
    x = layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(LSTM_UNITS))(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=arm.replace(" ", "_").replace("(", "").replace(")", ""))
    model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model

for arm in ARMS:
    m = build_model(arm)
    trainable = sum(np.prod(w.shape) for w in m.trainable_weights)
    total = sum(np.prod(w.shape) for w in m.weights)
    print(f"{arm:20s} total params = {total:>9,}   trainable = {trainable:>9,}")
build_model("GloVe (frozen)").summary()

Training protocol (identical for every run)¶

  • Optimiser RMSprop (lr = 1e-3), binary cross-entropy, batch size 32.

  • Early stopping on validation accuracy with restore_best_weights=True. This plays the same role as ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True) in the slides.

  • The epoch budget scales with data size. With 100 reviews an epoch is only 4 gradient steps, so the model needs many epochs before it moves off chance. With 20,000 reviews it overfits after a few.

    | training reviews | max epochs | patience | warm-up (no early stop before) | |---|---|---|---| | ≤ 250 | 60 | 10 | 10 | | ≤ 1,000 | 40 | 6 | 5 | | ≤ 5,000 | 20 | 4 | – | | > 5,000 | 12 | 3 | – |

    I added the warm-up after a first trial run. Without it, early stopping ended one 100-review learned-embedding run at epoch 6 while it was still at chance. Another seed that trained for the full budget reached 61%, so a short budget would have been unfair to the learned embedding.

  • Each run reports validation accuracy (10,000 reviews) and test accuracy (10,000 untouched reviews) of the restored best model.

In [14]:
def epoch_budget(n):
    """(max_epochs, patience, warm-up epochs before early stopping may trigger)"""
    if n <= 250:  return 60, 10, 10
    if n <= 1000: return 40, 6, 5
    if n <= 5000: return 20, 4, 0
    return 12, 3, 0

def train_subset(n, seed):
    """Seed-specific permutation of the pool; the first n items. Subsets are nested for a given seed."""
    p = np.random.default_rng(1000 + seed).permutation(len(X_pool))[:n]
    return X_pool[p], y_pool[p]

def run(arm, n, seed, verbose=0):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    X_tr, y_tr = train_subset(n, seed)
    max_epochs, patience, warmup = epoch_budget(n)
    model = build_model(arm)
    es = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_accuracy", patience=patience, start_from_epoch=warmup,
                                       restore_best_weights=True, mode="max")
    t0 = time.time()
    hist = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=max_epochs,
                     batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, validation_batch_size=512, callbacks=[es], verbose=verbose)
    if n == max(SIZES) and seed == 0 and arm != "GloVe (frozen)":
        np.save(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, f"embedding_{arm.split()[0].lower()}_{n}.npy"),
                model.layers[1].get_weights()[0])
    val_loss, val_acc = model.evaluate(X_val, y_val, batch_size=512, verbose=0)
    test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, batch_size=512, verbose=0)
    res = dict(arm=arm, n_train=n, seed=seed, val_acc=val_acc, val_loss=val_loss,
               test_acc=test_acc, best_epoch=int(np.argmax(hist.history["val_accuracy"]) + 1),
               epochs_run=len(hist.history["loss"]), train_acc_at_best=float(
                   hist.history["accuracy"][int(np.argmax(hist.history["val_accuracy"]))]),
               seconds=round(time.time() - t0, 1))
    return res, hist.history

4. Experiment 1: the assignment setting¶

100 training reviews, 150 words per review, top 10,000 words, 10,000 validation reviews. All three embedding versions are trained on the same 100 reviews with the same seed.

What Experiment 1 shows. With exactly 100 training reviews, all three models do better than chance (50%) but are far from good:

Embedding Validation acc. Test acc. Training acc. at best epoch
Learned embedding 63.5% 63.4% 100%
GloVe (frozen) 61.4% 60.8% 90%
GloVe (fine-tuned) 61.5% 61.2% 96%

So in the exact setting the assignment asks for, the embedding layer trained from scratch did slightly better than the pretrained GloVe embedding. I did not expect this, because the textbook suggests pretrained embeddings help most when there is very little data.

Figure 2 shows why the numbers are low. Training accuracy goes to 90-100% while validation accuracy stays in the low 60s, so every model is mostly memorising the 100 reviews. Frozen GloVe overfits a little less because only about 34,000 of its parameters can change, but that did not turn into higher validation accuracy.

A gap of about 2 points from one run is not strong evidence. Experiment 2 repeats every setting with different seeds and training subsets to check whether this result holds.

5. Experiment 2: how many training samples before the embedding layer wins?¶

Design.

  • Training-set sizes: 25, 50, 100, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, 20,000 (roughly log-spaced). I added 25 and 50 after the first results showed the learned embedding already ahead at 100 samples, which means any crossover has to be below the assignment setting.
  • Every other setting stays the same: same 10,000 validation reviews, 150-word cutoff, 10,000-word vocabulary, architecture and training protocol.
  • Repeated seeds (3 seeds for n ≤ 5,000, 2 for 10,000, 1 for 20,000). Each seed draws a different training subset and different initial weights. With 100 reviews, run-to-run variation is several percentage points, so a single run per size could not separate the methods reliably.
  • Results are appended to results/sweep_results.csv as each run finishes, so the cell can resume if interrupted.
In [17]:
def seeds_for(n):
    return [0, 1, 2] if n <= 5000 else ([0, 1] if n <= 10000 else [0])

sweep_csv = os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "sweep_results.csv")
done = pd.read_csv(sweep_csv) if os.path.exists(sweep_csv) else pd.DataFrame()
print(f"Runs already in {sweep_csv}: {len(done)} (loaded from cache, not re-trained)")
t_start = time.time()
for n in SIZES:
    for seed in seeds_for(n):
        for arm in ARMS:
            if len(done) and ((done.arm == arm) & (done.n_train == n) & (done.seed == seed)).any():
                continue
            res, _ = run(arm, n, seed)
            done = pd.concat([done, pd.DataFrame([res])], ignore_index=True)
            done.to_csv(sweep_csv, index=False)
            print(f"n={n:>6,} seed={seed} {arm:20s} val={res['val_acc']:.4f} test={res['test_acc']:.4f} "
                  f"best_ep={res['best_epoch']:>2}  ({res['seconds']:.0f}s, elapsed {(time.time()-t_start)/60:.1f} min)")
sweep = done.copy()
print("Total runs:", len(sweep))

5.2 Locating the crossover point¶

In [20]:
diff = (wide["Learned embedding"] - wide["GloVe (frozen)"])
# per-seed paired differences (same subset & seed for both arms)
paired = sweep.pivot_table(index=["n_train", "seed"], columns="arm", values="val_acc")
paired["diff"] = paired["Learned embedding"] - paired["GloVe (frozen)"]
paired_stats = paired.groupby("n_train")["diff"].agg(["mean", "min", "max", "count"])
paired_stats["learned wins (seeds)"] = paired.groupby("n_train")["diff"].apply(lambda d: f"{(d > 0).sum()}/{len(d)}")
print("Learned − GloVe(frozen), paired by seed (validation accuracy, percentage points):")
display((paired_stats[["mean", "min", "max"]] * 100).round(2).join(paired_stats[["learned wins (seeds)"]]))

# Linear interpolation of the crossover on a log-n scale
cross = None
xs, ds = np.log10(diff.index.values.astype(float)), diff.values
for i in range(len(ds) - 1):
    if ds[i] <= 0 < ds[i + 1]:
        cross = 10 ** (xs[i] + (0 - ds[i]) * (xs[i + 1] - xs[i]) / (ds[i + 1] - ds[i]))
first_win = next((n for n, d in zip(diff.index, ds) if d > 0 and all(ds[list(diff.index).index(n):] > 0)), None)
print(f"\nInterpolated crossover (log scale): ~{cross:,.0f} training samples" if cross else "\nNo sign change found")
print(f"Smallest tested size from which the learned embedding stays ahead: {first_win:,}" if first_win else "")

5.3 Validation vs. test accuracy (sanity check)¶

The best epoch is chosen on the validation set, so validation accuracy can be slightly optimistic. The untouched test set checks this.

In [23]:
chk = summary.copy(); chk["gap (val − test, pp)"] = (chk.val_mean - chk.test_mean) * 100
print(f"Mean |val − test| gap over all {len(chk)} cells: {chk['gap (val − test, pp)'].abs().mean():.2f} pp; "
      f"max {chk['gap (val − test, pp)'].abs().max():.2f} pp")
best = summary.loc[summary.val_mean.idxmax()]
print(f"Best configuration overall: {best.arm} with {int(best.n_train):,} training reviews -> "
      f"validation {best.val_mean:.2%}, test {best.test_mean:.2%}")

5.4 More views of the results¶

The next figures look at the same runs from different angles: run-to-run spread, overfitting, how well validation agrees with test, and training cost.

5.5 What did the embeddings learn?¶

To see why the two kinds of embedding behave differently, I compare the word vectors themselves: the frozen GloVe vectors and the learned embedding from the 20,000-review run (seed 0). For a few words I list the nearest neighbours by cosine similarity. I also project a set of sentiment words and plain topic words to 2-D with PCA.

In [29]:
word_to_id = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
emb_learned = np.load(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, f"embedding_learned_{max(SIZES)}.npy"))
emb_tuned = np.load(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, f"embedding_glove_{max(SIZES)}.npy"))

def neighbours(E, word, k=6):
    En = E / (np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
    sims = En @ En[word_to_id[word]]
    order = [i for i in np.argsort(-sims) if i > 1 and i != word_to_id[word]][:k]
    return ", ".join(vocab[i] for i in order)

probe = ["excellent", "awful", "boring", "masterpiece", "waste", "actor"]
pd.DataFrame({"GloVe (frozen)": [neighbours(embedding_matrix, w) for w in probe],
              "GloVe fine-tuned (20k)": [neighbours(emb_tuned, w) for w in probe],
              "Learned (20k)": [neighbours(emb_learned, w) for w in probe]}, index=probe)

def separation(E):
    Ep = E[[word_to_id[w] for w in pos_words]]; En_ = E[[word_to_id[w] for w in neg_words]]
    cos = lambda a, b: (a @ b.T) / (np.linalg.norm(a, axis=1)[:, None] * np.linalg.norm(b, axis=1)[None, :])
    within = (cos(Ep, Ep)[np.triu_indices(len(Ep), 1)].mean() + cos(En_, En_)[np.triu_indices(len(En_), 1)].mean()) / 2
    across = cos(Ep, En_).mean()
    return within, across
for name, E in [("GloVe (frozen)", embedding_matrix), ("GloVe fine-tuned", emb_tuned), ("Learned", emb_learned)]:
    w_, a_ = separation(E)
    print(f"{name:18s} mean cosine within same sentiment = {w_:.3f} | between positive and negative = {a_:.3f} | difference = {w_ - a_:.3f}")

6. Conclusions¶

6.1 Summary of results (validation accuracy on 10,000 reviews, mean over seeds)¶

Training reviews Learned embedding GloVe (frozen) GloVe (fine-tuned) Learned minus frozen GloVe
25 56.3% 54.4% 54.9% +1.9
50 59.7% 57.2% 57.1% +2.5
100 (assignment) 64.3% 59.9% 59.7% +4.3
500 72.9% 69.4% 69.1% +3.5
1,000 76.6% 71.7% 75.2% +5.0
2,000 79.2% 74.6% 79.2% +4.6
5,000 82.2% 79.7% 82.5% +2.5
10,000 83.3% 81.5% 83.2% +1.7
20,000 85.4% 83.9% 86.3% +1.5

Best result overall: GloVe (fine-tuned) with 20,000 reviews, 86.3% validation accuracy and 85.9% test accuracy.

6.2 Which approach did better, and at what point does the embedding layer win?¶

  1. In the assignment setting (100 reviews), the learned embedding layer did better than the pretrained GloVe embedding. Over three seeds it averaged 64.3% against 59.9% for frozen GloVe, and it won on every seed (Figure 4).
  2. I could not find a crossover point. The question assumes GloVe starts ahead and the embedding layer catches up as data grows. In my runs the learned embedding was never behind frozen GloVe on average, even with 25 training reviews. It won 2 of 3 seeds at 25 reviews and every seed from 50 reviews up. So if a point exists where frozen GloVe is better, it is below 25 reviews, where every model is close to guessing. The size of the advantage does change: it grows to about 5 points at 1,000-2,000 reviews and then shrinks to 1.5 points at 20,000, as both models approach the limit of what a 150-word review allows.
  3. Fine-tuning GloVe is the best option once there is enough data. Up to 500 reviews, fine-tuned GloVe behaves almost exactly like frozen GloVe, because there is too little signal to move the vectors much. From about 1,000 reviews it catches up with the learned embedding, and at 5,000 and 20,000 reviews it is the best of the three.
  4. The pretrained embedding is less reliable with little data. Figure 5 shows that frozen GloVe varies much more from seed to seed. At 100 reviews its range was 5.7 points, compared with 1.8 for the learned embedding.
  5. The validation numbers can be trusted. Validation and test accuracy differ by 0.45 points on average and never by more than 1.1 points (Figure 7). Picking the best epoch on the validation set did not inflate the results.

6.3 Why did the pretrained embedding not help more?¶

The word-vector analysis in section 5.5 explains most of it. GloVe was trained on Wikipedia and news text, where words are similar if they appear in similar contexts, not if they carry the same sentiment. In GloVe the nearest neighbours of "boring" include "funny", and "excellent" sits close to "good" and "quality". The average cosine similarity between positive and negative words (0.37) is not much lower than within the same sentiment (0.53), so the separation is only 0.16. The LSTM on top has to recover sentiment from vectors that were never organised around it, using only about 34,000 trainable weights.

The learned embedding does the opposite. Even from a few hundred reviews, the main thing it learns is a positive-to-negative axis. In the 20,000-review model the separation is 1.68, and positive and negative words point in opposite directions (Figure 10). The cost is that it loses general meaning: the nearest neighbours of "actor" in the learned space are "worst", "awful" and "poor", because the word mostly shows up in negative reviews. Fine-tuned GloVe sits in between. It keeps the general structure ("actor" stays next to "actress") and still more than doubles the sentiment separation, to 0.35. That combination is probably why it scored best once enough data was available.

Two choices in this setup also work against GloVe compared with the textbook example: reviews are cut to 150 words, and about 2% of the vocabulary (mostly names and misspellings) has no GloVe vector, so those words stay at zero.

6.4 Improving performance with limited data (MLO 4)¶

  • More labelled data is by far the biggest lever. Going from 100 to 20,000 reviews moved accuracy from about 64% to 85-86%, much more than any embedding choice.
  • A frozen pretrained embedding is not automatically a fix for small data. It only helps if the pretraining matches the task. Here it overfit less (Figure 6) but still generalised worse.
  • Fine-tuning a pretrained embedding was the best option from about 1,000 reviews upward.
  • Training details matter a lot when data is tiny. Without the warm-up before early stopping, some 100-review runs were stopped while still at chance. With only one run per setting, the seed-to-seed noise (up to 9.5 points at 25 reviews) would have been large enough to reverse some conclusions.
  • Accuracy ceiling. No model reached 90%. With 150-word reviews, about 60% of reviews are truncated and part of the opinion is thrown away. The textbook bidirectional LSTM reaches about 87-88% with 600-word reviews and the full 20,000-25,000 training set, so 86% at 150 words is close to what this architecture can do.

6.5 RNNs vs. Transformers (MLO 2 and 3)¶

The model here is a bidirectional LSTM, an RNN that reads the review one word at a time and passes a hidden state forward (and, in the second direction, backward). That makes it naturally order-aware, but it is slow to train because the steps cannot run in parallel, and information from early words fades over long sequences.

A Transformer replaces the recurrence with self-attention. Every word builds a query, a key and a value vector. Its new representation is a weighted average of all the value vectors in the sentence, where the weights come from how well its query matches each key. Because every word looks at every other word directly, long-range links like "not ... good" are one step apart instead of many, and the whole sequence is processed in parallel. Self-attention on its own ignores order, so positional embeddings are added to the word embeddings. The encoder stacks multi-head attention with feed-forward layers, residual connections and layer normalisation. The decoder adds masked self-attention and cross-attention for generating text.

For this assignment, the main practical difference is data. Transformers have many more parameters and usually need large datasets or large-scale pretraining to beat an LSTM. With 100 labelled reviews, a Transformer trained from scratch would overfit at least as badly as the LSTM did. A pretrained Transformer such as BERT, fine-tuned on these reviews, would likely be the strongest option for small data. It is the same idea as fine-tuning GloVe in section 6.4, but with a model that also brings pretrained knowledge of context and word order, not just individual word vectors.

6.6 Limitations¶

  • One architecture (BiLSTM with 32 units) and one optimiser setting. A different model, for example a smaller learned embedding or more dropout, could change the size of the gaps.
  • 20,000 reviews was run with a single seed and 10,000 with two, so the differences at the large end (about 1 point) are less certain than at the small end.
  • The vocabulary was built from the text (not the labels) of the 30,000-review training pool, so that the top-10,000-words requirement could be met for every training size. A model trained on only 100 reviews therefore knows the index of words it has never seen labelled. Those words carry no learned information for the learned embedding, but they do get GloVe vectors, which if anything helps GloVe.
